   Observed      g000021 (12:00, as unknown): App "Shiny \x1b[31mDocs" (client id
                 123456789012-k3v9qz7x2m4n8p1r5t6w0y3b7d9f2h4j.apps.googleusercontent.com) holds
                 access that can read drive.readonly and can change drive through grants from 2
                 active accounts: admin@example.com (super administrator), carol@example.com. The
                 name is chosen by whoever registered the app; it does not show who made it.
   Severity      high: base medium, +1 attribute admin grantor (g000020: admin@example.com is a
                 super administrator and granted this app the scope drive: whoever controls the app
                 can use those scopes as admin@example.com, though not that account's other
                 administrator rights.)
   Why here      admin@example.com is a super administrator and granted this app the scope drive:
                 whoever controls the app can use those scopes as admin@example.com, though not that
                 account's other administrator rights.
   Not checked   When each app was authorized or last used, and what it did with its access, were
                 not checked.
   Fix           Confirm someone in the company chose this app and still needs it. If not, remove
                 its access: an administrator can block it under Security → Access and data control
                 → API controls → Manage Third-Party App Access, and each person can remove it at
                 myaccount.google.com/permissions. If it is needed, configure it deliberately on
                 that page: Limited or Specific Google data where it still works, Trusted only if it
                 must reach services you restricted. Trusted widens what the app may reach; it does
                 not limit it, and this finding stays open either way. Prefer a version that asks
                 for less (for example, access to its own files instead of all of Drive). To keep it
                 as it is, accept it by its client id.

NOTES FOR THE READOUT
  saas:google-workspace:example.com: Returned credential permissions are unknown; effective
    permissions were not tested.
  saas:google-workspace:example.com: domains: observed 2; organizational units: observed 3;
    accounts: observed 6. Inventory alone does not assess account security or administrator access.
  saas:google-workspace:example.com: scheck could not identify the Google account used for this run.
    Information from earlier Workspace reads was not used in this report.
  saas:google-workspace:example.com: The separate token scheck used for the app check holds
    admin.directory.user.security, which also lets it revoke app access and app passwords, read or
    create backup codes, sign people out and turn off 2-step verification. scheck sent only the
    declared reads; effective access was not tested. If you will not run the app check again, remove
    that permission from the credential's domain-wide delegation entry or consent.
  saas:google-workspace:example.com: Checked: the apps each account authorized with its Google
    account and the access Google reports they hold. Not checked: domain-wide delegation,
    service-account keys, apps an administrator installed for everyone from Marketplace (they may
    not appear as a person's grant), app passwords, when each app was authorized or last used, and
    what any app did with its access.
  saas:google-workspace:example.com: 1 app holds scopes scheck does not classify and none it
    classifies as broad, so it was not judged: "Google Chrome"
    (77185425430.apps.googleusercontent.com). Its name is chosen by whoever registered it. Check
    under Security → Access and data control → API controls → Manage Third-Party App Access in the
    Admin console that someone chose it.
  saas:google-workspace:example.com: Mail forwarding was not checked. It finds mailboxes that send
    copies of mail to outside addresses, a common way an attacker keeps reading someone's mail after
    the password is changed. It needs a Google service account with domain-wide delegation for
    gmail.readonly, which can read every message; most small companies do not have one, and whoever
    manages your Google setup (often your IT provider) would create it. scheck signs in as each
    active mailbox and reads only its forwarding settings and filters, never a message. Whoever
    approves access to staff mailboxes must approve it and add authorization.mailboxes (asset, by,
    date, expires) to the engagement file first, then run with that service account's key file and
    SCHECK_WORKSPACE_PROFILE=directory_oauth_mail.
